newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi lawyer to see British nurses in murder case.
newsitem.headline: Saudi lawyer to see British nurses in murder case.

text.p: The Saudi Arabian lawyer providing legal advice for two British nurses charged with murder in the kingdom said on Wednesday he would make his first visit to the jailed women in three days' time.
Deborah Kim Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, have been charged with murdering Australian nurse Yvonne Gilford, 55, at the hospital complex in eastern Saudi Arabia where they worked.
The two were arrested and jailed in the nearby city of Dammam on December 20, nine days after Gilford was found stabbed and bludgeoned to death.

"Lawyers from my office are going to Dammam on Saturday...I will also go of course," Salah al-Hejailan told Reuters. "They will make the preliminary interviews, take down the circumstances, prepare the basic things."
If found guilty, the women could face public execution by the sword, according to Islamic sharia law.
Hejailan said that if the dealth penalty were imposed, it would be the first time foreign women were executed in the conservative kingdom.
But he said that even if the women were found guilty, a death sentence was unlikely.
Hejailan's firm said that under Islamic sharia law in force in the kingdom, the victim's family could ask for blood money which would spare the suspects' lives.
Under sharia, the victim's family, regardles of religion or nationality, can ask for the death sentence to be dropped in return for financial settlement, called 'diah' or blood money.
The family could also waive the right to blood money, in which case the court would decide on a sentence, which in such cases is usually five years imprisonment, the firm said.
"The death sentence will have to be asked for by the victim's family. If the family of the victim does not ask for it, the Saudi judge will not order it," Hejailan said.
"Even if the family wants the death penalty, the judge will have to evaluate the circumstances," he said.
The head of state has the right to cancel the sentence.
Hejailan said sharia law would ensure the nurses receive a fair trial, adding the case was an opportunity for the world to learn about Saudi Arabia's legal system.
"I will plead the case in court out loud and in writing. There will be cross-examination of the witnesses. It is almost the same system as in the West," he said.
British consul Tim Lamb visited the jail in Dammam on Monday and met the women separately for 15 minutes each.
"Both women seemed in good health but were obviously concerned about the charges levelled against them," he said.
